questions.q: Per this lesson, does building a technically sound catalog guarantee people will actually use it?
options: No — adoption is a separate, harder problem that technical quality alone doesn't solve
Yes — technical quality automatically guarantees adoption
Yes, but only for catalogs built after 2020
No one has ever successfully adopted a data catalog
questions.explain: Scanning, curating, linking, and search are necessary but not sufficient — adoption is the separate problem that determines whether the technical work pays off.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three adoption barriers named in this lesson?
options: Habit — people's existing, faster-for-now workaround competing against the new tool
The catalog software's exact version number
The number of fonts used in the catalog's interface
Whether the catalog was built on a weekday or weekend
questions.explain: The three barriers are habit, trust, and visibility — habit specifically means an old method (asking a colleague, a spreadsheet) that's faster right now, even if the catalog is objectively better.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what typically happens after someone gets one stale or wrong result from the catalog?
options: They often conclude the catalog isn't reliable and go back to their old method, sometimes permanently
They automatically report the error and nothing else changes
The catalog software deletes itself
They are legally required to keep using the catalog regardless
questions.explain: This is the trust barrier — one bad experience, directly caused by a metadata quality failure like those described in Lesson 23, can permanently end someone's willingness to use the catalog.

questions.q: What tactic does this lesson suggest for the 'habit' barrier specifically?
options: Integrate the catalog into existing workflows, like embedding search directly in the BI tool people already open daily
Force every employee to attend a mandatory multi-day training course
Delete all alternative methods of finding data
Increase the number of fields required on every catalog entry
questions.explain: A catalog embedded where people already work beats a separate destination nobody remembers to visit — meeting people where their habit already is.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do most failed metadata programs actually fail?
options: Because nobody treated adoption as its own deliberate workstream, not because the underlying technology was wrong
Because database servers are inherently unreliable
Because metadata programs are illegal in most countries
Because catalogs can only ever support one user at a time
questions.explain: Getting a hundred people to change a habit is harder than getting a database to return correct search results — treating adoption as an afterthought is the real risk.
